lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Heat and temperature: meaning, units, differences and effects of heat
objectives: Distinguish between heat and temperature.
Convert between the Celsius and Kelvin scales.
State the effects of heat on a body.
lessons.body:
HEAT is a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference. Its SI unit is the joule (J). TEMPERATURE tells how hot or cold a body is; it is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. Its SI unit is the kelvin (K); the Celsius scale (°C) is also used. Heat is measured with a calorimeter; temperature is measured with a thermometer.

DIFFERENCES. (1) Heat is energy (joules); temperature is a degree of hotness (kelvin or °C). (2) Heat depends on the mass and the substance as well as the temperature; temperature does not depend on the amount of substance. (3) Heat flows because of a temperature difference; temperature is the property that decides the direction of the flow.
Example: a bucket of warm water and a cup of warm water at 40 °C have the same temperature, but the bucket holds more heat energy because it has more mass.

SCALES. T(K) = θ(°C) + 273. Example 1: 27 °C = 300 K. Example 2: 350 K = 77 °C. The temperature difference is the same on both scales: a rise of 10 °C is a rise of 10 K.

EFFECTS OF HEAT. When heat is added to a body: (1) its temperature rises; (2) it expands; (3) it may change state (melting, boiling, evaporation); (4) a metal heated to a high temperature can emit electrons (thermionic emission); (5) chemical changes can occur (e.g. cooking, burning).
Example 3 (heat gained). The heat needed to raise the temperature of a mass m of a substance by Δθ is Q = mcΔθ, where c is the specific heat capacity (water: about 4200 J/kg °C). For 2 kg of water heated from 20 °C to 30 °C: Q = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84 000 J.

practice.question: Convert 47 °C to kelvin and 250 K to °C.
State three differences between heat and temperature.
practice.answer: Heat is energy in joules, temperature is hotness in K or °C; heat depends on mass, temperature does not; heat flows because of temperature difference.

practice.question: Name four effects of heat on a body.
practice.answer: Rise in temperature, expansion, change of state, thermionic emission (or chemical change).

practice.question: Find the heat needed to raise 0.5 kg of water from 25 °C to 85 °C (c = 4200 J/kg °C).

marking.criterion: 1 mark formula, 1 mark substitution, 1 mark answer with unit.

practice.question: Why does the bucket of warm water hold more heat than the cup at the same temperature?
practice.answer: It has more mass, hence more molecules each carrying energy.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Thermal expansion of solids: effects, applications and a simple calculation
objectives: Explain why solids expand on heating.
Describe applications and disadvantages of thermal expansion.
Calculate a change in length.
lessons.body:
WHY SOLIDS EXPAND. The molecules of a solid vibrate about fixed positions. When the solid is heated they vibrate with larger amplitude, so the average distance between them increases and the solid expands. When it cools it contracts. Different solids expand by different amounts.

LINEAR EXPANSION. The increase in length ΔL of a rod of original length L₀ for a temperature rise Δθ is ΔL = αL₀Δθ, where α is the linear expansivity of the material (unit per kelvin, K⁻¹). New length L = L₀(1 + αΔθ).
Example 1. A steel rail 20 m long, α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, warms by 40 K: ΔL = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 20 × 40 = 9.6 × 10⁻³ m = 9.6 mm. Gaps are left between rails for this reason.
Example 2. An aluminium rod 5 m long, α = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, is heated by 60 K: ΔL = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ × 5 × 60 = 6.9 × 10⁻³ m, so the new length is 5.0069 m.

APPLICATIONS (useful). Bimetallic strip: two metals (e.g. brass and iron) joined together bend when heated because one expands more than the other; used in thermostats, fire alarms and flashers. Tight-fitting rims on wheels and red-hot rivets in ship building: the metal is put on hot and contracts to hold tightly.
DISADVANTAGES and design precautions. Bridges rest on rollers at one end and concrete roads have gaps so that expansion does not cause buckling; overhead cables sag in hot weather; glass cracks if hot liquid is poured into it suddenly because the inner wall expands before the outer; pipes can burst or leak when they expand and contract repeatedly.

practice.question: Why are small gaps left between sections of a railway track?
practice.answer: So that the rails can expand in hot weather without buckling.

practice.question: A copper rod 2 m long (α = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) is heated through 50 K. Find the increase in length.

marking.criterion: 1 mark formula, 1 mark substitution, 1 mark answer with unit.

practice.question: Why does a thick glass tumbler crack if boiling water is poured in suddenly?
practice.answer: The inner surface expands first while the outer surface is still cool; the uneven expansion cracks the glass.

practice.question: Explain how a bimetallic strip bends when heated.
practice.answer: The two metals expand by different amounts; the metal that expands more is on the outside of the curve.

practice.question: A bar of length 3 m at 20 °C has α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Find its length at 120 °C.

marking.criterion: 1 mark Δθ, 1 mark ΔL, 1 mark L.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: The fuse: ratings, fusing factor and choosing a fuse
objectives: Define a fuse, current rating, fusing current and fusing factor.
Choose a suitable fuse for an appliance.
List types of fuse and ways of detecting faults.
lessons.body:
A FUSE is a safety device placed in an electric circuit. It contains a thin wire (the fuse element) that heats up and melts when too much current flows, opening the circuit and protecting the appliance and wiring from damage or fire. A fuse is always fitted in the LIVE wire.

TERMS. Current rating: the largest current the fuse can carry continuously without melting. Fusing current: the smallest current that will melt the element. Fusing factor = fusing current ÷ current rating (always more than 1).
Example 1. A fuse has a rating of 10 A and a fusing current of 15 A: fusing factor = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5.

CHOOSING A FUSE. Find the normal working current I = P ÷ V and choose the fuse whose rating is just above it.
Example 2. A 1.5 kW electric iron works from a 240 V supply. I = 1500 ÷ 240 = 6.25 A. Available ratings: 3 A, 5 A, 10 A, 13 A. The 3 A and 5 A fuses are too low and would blow; choose the 10 A fuse.
Example 3. A 60 W lamp on 240 V draws 60 ÷ 240 = 0.25 A, so a 3 A fuse is suitable.

TYPES. Rewirable fuse (element can be replaced), cartridge fuse (sealed glass or ceramic tube), high breaking-capacity fuse (for large fault currents).
DETECTING FAULTS in a circuit. Continuity tester (is the circuit complete?), insulation-resistance tester (is there leakage through insulation?), polarity test with a test lamp or bell (is the switch in the live wire?), earth-loop impedance tester (is the earth connection good?).

practice.question: Define fusing factor and calculate it for a fuse rated 5 A that blows at 8 A.
practice.answer: Fusing current ÷ current rating = 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6.

practice.question: A 2.4 kW heater works from 240 V. Calculate the working current and suggest a fuse from 5 A, 10 A, 13 A, 30 A.
practice.answer: I = 2400 ÷ 240 = 10 A; choose 13 A (a 10 A fuse has no margin).

marking.criterion: 1 mark current, 1 mark choice with reason.

practice.question: Why is a fuse placed in the live wire?
practice.answer: So that the appliance is disconnected from the live supply when the fuse blows.

practice.question: List three types of fuse.
practice.answer: Rewirable, cartridge, high breaking-capacity.

practice.question: Name two instruments used to test a fuse or check the continuity of its circuit.
practice.answer: A continuity tester and a Megger (insulation-resistance tester).

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Surface tension: meaning, effects, applications and reduction
objectives: Define surface tension and state its unit.
Explain surface tension using molecular forces.
Describe effects, applications and ways of reducing surface tension.
lessons.body:
MEANING. Inside a liquid each molecule is pulled equally in all directions by its neighbours. A molecule at the surface has neighbours only below and beside it, so there is a net pull inward. The surface therefore behaves like a stretched elastic skin that tries to have the smallest possible area. SURFACE TENSION γ is the force acting along the surface, at right angles to a line of unit length: γ = F/L. Its unit is newton per metre (N/m). For a soap film on a wire frame the film has two surfaces, so F = 2γL, i.e. γ = F/2L.
Example 1. A soap film on a frame 5 cm (0.05 m) wide pulls with a force of 2.0 × 10⁻³ N. γ = F/2L = 2.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ (2 × 0.05) = 0.02 N/m.
Example 2. Water has γ = 0.072 N/m. The pull on 8 cm (0.08 m) of its surface (one surface): F = γL = 0.072 × 0.08 = 5.8 × 10⁻³ N.

EFFECTS. Soap bubbles and small droplets are spherical (a sphere has the smallest area for its volume); water striders walk on water; a clean needle or razor blade placed gently on water floats; mercury spilled on glass forms spherical beads.
APPLICATIONS. Waterproofing of cloth (the pores do not wet), blotting paper and wicks, the rise of molten wax up a candle wick.
REDUCING SURFACE TENSION. Add soap, detergent, alcohol or similar impurities; heat the liquid (γ falls as temperature rises). This is why detergent helps to wash grease off cloth: the liquid spreads and wets better.

practice.question: Define surface tension and give its SI unit.
practice.answer: The force per unit length acting along the surface of a liquid; N/m.

practice.question: Why are small drops of liquid spherical?
practice.answer: Surface tension makes the surface contract to the smallest area; a sphere has the least surface for a given volume.

practice.question: A soap film on a frame 6 cm wide pulls with a force of 3.0 × 10⁻³ N. Find γ.

marking.criterion: 1 mark formula, 1 mark substitution, 1 mark answer with unit.

practice.question: State three ways of reducing surface tension and two applications.
practice.answer: Add soap/detergent, add alcohol, heat; applications: waterproofing, blotting paper, wicks.

practice.question: A needle floats on water but sinks when a drop of detergent is added. Explain.
practice.answer: Detergent reduces the surface tension, so the surface skin can no longer support the needle's weight.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Capillarity: cohesion, adhesion and the rise or fall of liquids in narrow tubes
objectives: Distinguish between cohesion and adhesion.
Explain capillary rise and fall using molecular forces.
Give applications of capillarity.
lessons.body:
DEFINITIONS. Cohesion is the force of attraction between molecules of the SAME substance (e.g. water–water). Adhesion is the force of attraction between molecules of DIFFERENT substances (e.g. water–glass). Capillarity is the rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow (capillary) tube.

EXPLANATION (kinetic theory). In a glass tube dipped in water, the adhesion between water and glass molecules is stronger than the cohesion between water molecules. The water molecules at the wall are pulled up, the surface curves upward (concave meniscus), surface tension pulls the liquid up the tube, and it stops rising when the weight of the raised column balances the upward pull. In mercury the cohesion is stronger than the adhesion to glass, so the mercury surface curves downward (convex meniscus) and the level in the tube is DEPRESSED below the outside level. Water wets glass; mercury does not.

NARROWER TUBES. The narrower the tube, the greater the rise. Worked example: if water rises 30 mm in a tube of radius 0.5 mm, then in a tube of radius 1 mm (twice as wide) it rises about 15 mm, because the rise is inversely proportional to the radius (an experimental result; the full formula is beyond this lesson).

APPLICATIONS. Oil rising up a lamp wick; a towel or blotting paper soaking up a spill; water rising from the soil through the fine tubes in plant roots and stems; ink flowing in a pen nib. Capillarity in building walls causes damp, which is why damp-proof courses are laid.

practice.question: Differentiate between cohesion and adhesion.
practice.answer: Cohesion: attraction between like molecules; adhesion: attraction between unlike molecules.

practice.question: Explain why water rises in a glass capillary tube.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Motion, force and circular motion
objectives: Define motion and classify common types of motion, including translational, rotational, oscillatory, random and relative motion.
Define force and distinguish contact forces from field forces.
Describe uniform circular motion and identify the direction of tangential velocity and centripetal acceleration.
Calculate centripetal acceleration and force using the mass, speed and radius of a moving body.
Explain centrifugal force as an apparent inertial effect in a rotating frame of reference.
lessons.body:
Motion is a change in the position of a body with time, described relative to a reference point. A body may be at rest relative to one observer and moving relative to another. For example, a learner seated in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but moves relative to the road.

TYPES OF MOTION
- Translational motion: a body moves from one place to another; all points of the body move through corresponding distances in the same direction at a given instant. A car moving along a straight road is an example.
- Rotational motion: a body turns about an axis. A rotating fan is an example.
- Oscillatory motion: repeated to-and-fro motion about an equilibrium position. A simple pendulum moving through small angles is an example.
- Random motion: motion with no single fixed direction or regular path, such as dust particles moving irregularly in air.
- Relative motion: motion described in relation to a chosen observer or reference frame.

FORCE AND MOTION
A force is a push or pull. Force is a vector quantity and is measured in newtons (N). A resultant force can change a body's speed, direction of motion or shape. Contact forces act when bodies touch; examples include friction, tension and the normal reaction. Field forces act without direct contact; examples include gravitational, magnetic and electric forces.

CIRCULAR MOTION
Circular motion occurs when a body follows a circular path about a centre at a constant radius. In uniform circular motion, the speed may remain constant, but velocity changes because its direction changes continuously. At any point, the instantaneous velocity is along the tangent to the circle.

CENTRIPETAL ACCELERATION AND FORCE
The acceleration of a body moving in a circle is directed towards the centre. It is called centripetal acceleration:
ac = v²/r
where v is tangential speed in metres per second (m/s), r is radius in metres (m), and ac is in metres per second squared (m/s²).

The resultant inward force that keeps the body on the circular path is called centripetal force:
Fc = m ac = mv²/r
where m is mass in kilograms (kg) and Fc is in newtons (N). The centripetal force is not a separate new kind of force. It may be supplied by tension in a string, friction between tyres and a road, gravity, or a normal reaction, depending on the situation.

Worked example 1
A 0.5 kg object moves at 4 m/s in a circle of radius 2 m. Find its centripetal acceleration and centripetal force.
ac = v²/r = 4²/2 = 8 m/s².
Fc = m ac = 0.5 × 8 = 4 N.
The acceleration and resultant force point towards the centre.

CENTRIFUGAL EFFECT
A passenger in a turning bus may feel as if they are pushed outwards. In an inertial frame (for example, an observer standing by the road), the passenger tends to continue in a straight line unless an inward force changes the direction of motion. In the bus's rotating frame, an apparent outward inertial force is often called centrifugal force. It is useful to describe the sensation in that rotating frame, but it is not a real outward interaction acting on the passenger in the ground frame. Do not confuse this apparent outward effect with the real inward centripetal force that maintains circular motion.

Worked example 2
A 0.2 kg stone moves at 5 m/s in a circle of radius 0.5 m.
ac = v²/r = 5²/0.5 = 50 m/s².
Fc = m ac = 0.2 × 50 = 10 N.

Applications
- A string's tension can provide the centripetal force for a stone moving in a circle.
- Friction between a tyre and the road can provide the centripetal force when a car turns.
- Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps a satellite in orbit.
- A rotating washing machine or centrifuge uses rotation to separate materials.

Safety for a simple demonstration
If a teacher demonstrates circular motion with a light, securely tied stopper, use a clear area, keep learners outside the path, check the knot and string before starting, and stop the demonstration if the string or attachment is damaged. Never swing a heavy object or point it towards another person.

practice.answer: Motion is a change in position with time relative to a reference point. (a) Rotational, (b) oscillatory, (c) random, (d) translational.

practice.answer: Centripetal force is the real resultant force directed towards the centre that changes the passenger's direction and keeps the passenger moving along the curved path. lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Friction: types, effects, advantages and control
objectives: Define friction as a contact force that opposes relative motion or its tendency between surfaces in contact.
Distinguish static, sliding, rolling and fluid friction.
Explain common advantages and disadvantages of friction.
Describe practical methods of increasing or reducing friction.
Plan a simple safe investigation comparing friction on different surfaces.
lessons.body:
Friction is a contact force that opposes the relative motion, or the tendency of relative motion, between surfaces that touch. It acts along the surfaces and opposite to the direction in which the surfaces are sliding or trying to slide.

TYPES OF FRICTION
- Static friction acts between surfaces that are in contact but are not yet sliding. It can prevent a book from sliding down a slightly tilted desk.
- Sliding (kinetic) friction acts when one surface slides over another, such as a block being pulled across a table.
- Rolling friction acts when a wheel or ball rolls over a surface. It is usually less than sliding friction for the same pair of surfaces.
- Fluid friction (drag) acts when an object moves through a liquid or gas, such as air resistance on a moving bicycle.

WHAT AFFECTS FRICTION?
For dry surfaces, friction generally increases when the surfaces are pressed together more strongly. The nature of the surfaces also matters: rough or gripping surfaces usually provide more friction than smooth, well-lubricated surfaces. The exact force depends on the materials and conditions; do not assume that apparent contact area alone always determines dry friction.

ADVANTAGES OF FRICTION
- It allows people to walk without slipping.
- It enables tyres to grip the road and brakes to slow or stop a vehicle.
- It allows a pencil or chalk to leave marks on a surface.
- It helps a knot, screw or belt grip and remain in place.

DISADVANTAGES OF FRICTION
- It causes wear of moving machine parts, tyres and shoe soles.
- It produces unwanted heat and wastes useful energy.
- It can cause noise and reduce the efficiency of machines.

WAYS TO REDUCE FRICTION
- Apply suitable lubricants such as oil or grease between moving surfaces.
- Use ball bearings or rollers to replace sliding contact with rolling contact.
- Polish or smooth surfaces where appropriate.
- Streamline vehicles and other bodies moving through air or water to reduce fluid drag.
- Use an air cushion where the equipment is designed for it.

WAYS TO INCREASE FRICTION
- Make contact surfaces rougher or add suitable tread patterns.
- Use materials with better grip on shoe soles and tyres.
- Keep brake pads and friction surfaces clean and in good condition.
- Sprinkle sand or grit on a slippery surface when appropriate.

Worked example
A cyclist needs friction between the tyres and the road to move forward and to brake. If the road is wet or covered with loose sand, the available grip may be reduced, so the cyclist should reduce speed and avoid sudden braking or sharp turns. Friction is useful when controlled, but excessive or unwanted friction in machine parts causes wear and energy loss.

Simple classroom investigation
Place a wooden block on a level table and attach a spring balance. Pull horizontally and note the force just as the block begins to move. Repeat with a suitable smooth sheet placed under the block. Keep the block and spring balance in good condition, pull gently, and do not use heavy loads. Compare the readings to discuss how the contact surfaces affect the force needed to start motion.

practice.question: Define friction and state the direction in which it acts when two surfaces slide against each other.
practice.answer: Friction is a contact force that opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion between surfaces in contact. During sliding it acts along the surfaces opposite to the direction of sliding.

marking.criterion: Defines friction as a contact force between touching surfaces.
States that it opposes relative motion or its tendency.

practice.answer: (a) Static friction, (b) sliding friction, (c) rolling friction, (d) fluid friction (air resistance/drag).

practice.question: State two factors that affect friction between dry surfaces and give two ways of reducing unwanted friction.
practice.answer: Factors include the nature/roughness of the surfaces and how strongly they are pressed together. Friction can be reduced by lubrication, ball bearings/rollers, smoothing surfaces or streamlining to reduce air/water drag.

marking.criterion: States the nature/roughness of the surfaces.
Gives a second valid reduction method.

practice.question: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of friction.
practice.answer: Advantages: walking without slipping; tyres gripping the road/brakes stopping a vehicle; writing with pencil/chalk. Disadvantages: wear of moving parts; unwanted heat and energy loss; noise.

practice.question: Explain why tyres have tread patterns and why brakes need friction.
practice.answer: Tread patterns improve grip between the tyre and road, helping prevent slipping. Brakes use friction between the brake pad and rotating disc/drum to slow the wheel and vehicle.

marking.criterion: Explains brake friction slows the wheel/vehicle.

practice.question: In a simple friction investigation, a block is pulled with a spring balance. What should be recorded when the block just begins to move, and why might the reading change if the surface is changed?
practice.answer: Record the spring-balance force at the instant the block just begins to move; this estimates the limiting static friction. A different surface has a different nature/roughness and can produce a different friction force.

marking.criterion: Identifies the spring-balance force at the onset of motion.
Explains that changing surface material/roughness changes the friction.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Scalars, vectors and linear motion graphs
objectives: Distinguish scalar quantities from vector quantities.
Differentiate distance from displacement and speed from velocity.
Calculate average speed, average velocity and acceleration with correct SI units.
Apply the four equations of uniformly accelerated straight-line motion.
Interpret distance-time and displacement-time graphs using their gradients.
Interpret speed-time and velocity-time graphs using gradient and area.
lessons.body:
SCALAR AND VECTOR QUANTITIES
A scalar quantity has magnitude only. It does not require a direction to describe it. Examples include distance, speed, time, mass, temperature and energy.

A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. A vector should be stated with a direction, such as 5 m east or 12 m/s north.

DISTANCE AND DISPLACEMENT
Distance is the total length of the path travelled. It is a scalar and its SI unit is the metre (m).
Displacement is the straight-line change in position from the starting point to the finishing point, with direction. It is a vector and its SI unit is also the metre (m).
Distance is never less than the magnitude of displacement. If a person returns to the starting point, the total distance may be positive while the displacement is zero.

Example 1
A learner walks 3 m east and then 4 m west along the same straight path.
Distance = 3 + 4 = 7 m.
Taking east as positive, displacement = +3 − 4 = −1 m, which is 1 m west.

SPEED AND VELOCITY
Average speed is total distance divided by total time:
average speed = total distance / total time.
Speed is scalar and is measured in metres per second (m/s).

Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time:
average velocity = displacement / total time.
Velocity is a vector and must include direction. Its SI unit is m/s.

Example 2
A vehicle travels 180 m in 30 s.
Average speed = 180/30 = 6 m/s.

Example 3
A body moves 100 m east in 20 s.
Average velocity = 100/20 = 5 m/s east.

ACCELERATION AND RETARDATION
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity:
a = (v − u)/t
where u is initial velocity, v is final velocity and t is the time interval. The SI unit is m/s². Acceleration is a vector because velocity has direction.
Retardation (deceleration) is acceleration opposite to the chosen direction of motion; in a one-dimensional calculation it is often represented by a negative acceleration.

UNIFORMLY ACCELERATED MOTION
For motion in a straight line with constant acceleration:
1. v = u + at
2. s = ut + ½at²
3. v² = u² + 2as
4. s = ½(u + v)t
Here s is displacement in the chosen direction. In a straight journey without a change of direction, its magnitude equals the distance travelled.

Worked example 4
A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² for 8 s.
u = 0, a = 3 m/s², t = 8 s.
v = u + at = 0 + (3 × 8) = 24 m/s.
s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 3 × 8² = 96 m.

DISTANCE-TIME AND DISPLACEMENT-TIME GRAPHS
Time is plotted on the horizontal axis. Distance or displacement is plotted on the vertical axis.
- The gradient of a distance-time graph gives speed.
- The gradient of a displacement-time graph gives velocity, including its sign/direction.
- A horizontal line means the distance or displacement is not changing during that interval (the body is at rest relative to the reference point).
- A straight sloping line has a constant gradient and therefore represents constant speed or velocity.
- A curved line has a changing gradient and therefore represents changing speed or velocity.

SPEED-TIME AND VELOCITY-TIME GRAPHS
Time is plotted on the horizontal axis and speed or velocity on the vertical axis.
- The gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
- The area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement. If velocity remains positive, this area is also the distance travelled.
- The area under a speed-time graph gives distance travelled.
- A horizontal velocity-time line represents constant velocity and zero acceleration.
- A straight sloping velocity-time line represents uniform acceleration.

Worked example 5
A body increases its velocity uniformly from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s.
Acceleration = gradient = (20 − 0)/10 = 2 m/s².
Displacement = area under the velocity-time graph = ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m.

GRAPH AND UNIT CHECKS
- Use seconds (s) for time, metres (m) for distance/displacement, metres per second (m/s) for speed/velocity, and metres per second squared (m/s²) for acceleration.
- Label both graph axes and include units.
- A gradient is rise divided by run, with the units implied by the axes.
- Do not confuse the slope of a velocity-time graph (acceleration) with its area (displacement).
- For motion that reverses direction, displacement and velocity may be negative while distance and speed remain non-negative.

practice.question: Classify each quantity as scalar or vector: distance, speed, time, mass, displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. State the key difference between a scalar and a vector.
practice.answer: Scalars: distance, speed, time and mass. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.

marking.criterion: Defines vector as magnitude and direction.
Correctly classifies the four scalar quantities.
Correctly classifies the four vector quantities.

practice.question: A learner walks 3 m east and then 4 m west along the same straight path. Find the total distance and the displacement.
practice.answer: Distance = 3 + 4 = 7 m. Taking east as positive, displacement = 3 − 4 = −1 m = 1 m west.

practice.question: A vehicle travels 180 m in 30 s. Calculate its average speed. A second body moves 100 m east in 20 s; calculate its average velocity.
practice.answer: Average speed = 180/30 = 6 m/s. Average velocity = 100/20 = 5 m/s east.

marking.criterion: Uses total distance ÷ total time for average speed.
Uses displacement ÷ time for average velocity.

practice.question: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² for 8 s. Find its final velocity and displacement.
practice.answer: u = 0, a = 3 m/s², t = 8 s. v = u + at = 24 m/s. s = ut + ½at² = 96 m.

marking.criterion: Identifies u = 0, a = 3 m/s² and t = 8 s.

practice.question: A body's velocity increases uniformly from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s. Find (a) its acceleration and (b) its displacement during the 10 s.
practice.answer: Acceleration = gradient = (20 − 0)/10 = 2 m/s². Displacement = area under the velocity-time graph = ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m.

marking.criterion: Uses area of triangle under the velocity-time graph.

practice.question: State what the gradient represents on (a) a distance-time graph, (b) a displacement-time graph and (c) a velocity-time graph. State what the area under a velocity-time graph represents.
practice.answer: (a) Speed, (b) velocity, (c) acceleration. The area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement.
